questions.prompt: Which two numbers give a risk its rating?
options: Cost and speed of the fix
Ports and services open on it
Users and devices affected
Likelihood and impact

questions.prompt: A risk is both very likely and very damaging. Where does it go on the list?
options: In the middle
At the top
At the bottom
Off the list

questions.prompt: What does it mean to treat a risk?
options: Note it and move on
Wait for an attack first
Hand it to an insurer
Fix it yourself, now

questions.prompt: What does it mean to transfer a risk?
options: Write the risk down and decide to live with it
Fix the weakness yourself before the end of the day
Move the risky server to a different room
Hand the burden to someone better placed

questions.prompt: Which is an example of transferring a risk?
options: Buying insurance
Ignoring the risk
Changing a password
Deleting an account

questions.prompt: When is accepting a risk the right response?
options: When its impact is low
When nobody has rated it
When it is very likely

questions.prompt: The relay console still has its factory password. Likelihood high, impact high. Which response fits?

Ignore it

questions.prompt: Why rate risks before deciding what to do?
options: Only rated risks can be attacked
A crew cannot fix everything at once
Unrated risks are always low impact

questions.prompt: What is cybercrime?

A crime done using computers or networks
A business dispute between two companies
A software bug that crashes a program

questions.prompt: What is a ransomware attack?
options: Flooding a website with traffic
Holding files hostage for payment
Copying a file to sell it on
Sending fake emails to trick users

questions.prompt: Which Philippine law is an example of a cybercrime law?
options: Republic Act 10175
Republic Act 8293
Republic Act 10173
Republic Act 9995

questions.prompt: Why preserve evidence before restoring anything?
options: To keep proof of exactly what happened
To make the backup restore much faster
Because the attacker asked you to wait

questions.prompt: How do you preserve a file an attacker touched?
options: Hash it before you clean it up
Rename it so the attacker cannot find it
Email it to every member of the crew
Delete it before anyone else sees it

questions.prompt: Why should you never pay a ransom?
options: It is always cheaper to buy new computers instead
The attacker always gives the files back for free
It funds the next attack and guarantees nothing
Paying makes the files unreadable for good

questions.prompt: Instead of paying, how do you get scrambled files back?
options: Run the ransom program again
Restore from a clean backup
Ask the attacker for a discount

questions.prompt: When is the right moment to report a cyberattack to the authorities?
options: Before you even check what has happened
Once evidence is kept and service is back
Never, attacks are a private matter for the crew

questions.prompt: What is ITIL?
options: A cipher that shifts each letter by three places
A law that makes hacking a crime in the Philippines
A set of practices for running IT services well
A firewall rule that blocks every unused port

questions.prompt: What is change management?
options: A tool that changes files back by itself
A way to change passwords every day
A rule that no system may ever change
A process for making changes safely

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of change management?
options: Production, then test, then request
Test, production, then request
Request, production, then test
Request, test, then production

questions.prompt: Why file a change request first?
options: A request lets you skip the testing step entirely
The request makes the change happen faster on its own
It records what was intended and who approved it
Attackers cannot read a system with a change request

questions.prompt: Where should a change be tested?
options: On the live system everyone depends on
On the attacker's own computer
On a test system serving nobody yet
On a printed copy of the code

questions.prompt: A fix feels very urgent. What should happen?
options: It skips the request because it is urgent
It goes straight to production to save time
It still goes request, test, production

questions.prompt: What usually turns an urgent fix into an outage?
options: Testing the change on a separate test system
Skipping the test and going straight live
Writing down who approved the change beforehand
Following the change process in its usual order

questions.prompt: "I was sure it would work" is not the same as what?
options: I asked a friend
I ran it live
I wrote it
I tested it

questions.prompt: A risk has low impact but is very likely. Which response fits?
options: Accept it
Pay a ransom
Transfer it
Treat it now

questions.prompt: A risk has high impact, but the crew cannot fully own it alone. Which response fits?
options: Transfer it
Accept it
Ignore it
Hide it away

questions.prompt: Which is a correct statement about cybercrime?
options: It only counts if more than one computer is hit
It is a private dispute settled by payment

questions.prompt: Ransomware scrambles the supply logs. What is the first step?
options: Preserve the evidence

options: Nobody, approvals slow things down
